paras: The killing of Andrew Render was the fatal shooting of Andrew ("Andy") Render, a Black man, by town marshal R. L. Paris on the night of May 16, 1903, during the street fair in Hartford, Ohio County, Kentucky. Paris said Render had defied and advanced on him, and five days later a grand jury declined to indict the marshal. The first dispatch drew notice by describing armed Black and white crowds and a vow by white citizens that every Black person in the county would be "exterminated" if anyone tried to take Paris.

Hartford had held a street fair all week, drawing several hundred people that Saturday. By evening, the Hartford Herald said, a crowd of Black men from the mines at McHenry remained. Both the Louisville Courier-Journal and the Herald reported that Render had threatened the marshal in an earlier clash.

The trouble began when Pendleton Hudson, a white man, struck another white man, James Wysong, with a chair. In the Courier-Journal's version, a deputy fired at the fleeing Hudson, and about fifty Black men drinking in a nearby alley started toward the main street, where Paris faced them and threatened arrest. The Herald instead said Paris arrested Wysong and then followed a noisy group of Black men down an alley, warning that he would arrest some of them.

In the Herald's account, which came from Paris himself, Render stepped out of the crowd, said the marshal could not arrest him, and advanced "with one hand behind him." Paris, the paper said, feared for his life and shot Render through the heart. The Courier-Journal's correspondent had Render curse the marshal and reach toward his back pocket before Paris fired at close range. Paris went directly to the sheriff and gave himself up.

The Courier-Journal described some 150 Black men, many from the nearby coal mines, gathered in the alleys, with members of Render's lodge saying he had been "shot down for nothing" and that they would mob Paris. Fifty deputies were sworn in to guard Paris, about fifty more citizens patrolled the streets, and both sides were said to carry rifles, shotguns and pistols.

A Louisville dispatch the next day reported no further disorder and said the danger of Black residents trying "to lynch the officer" was apparently over. On May 21 the grand jury, already in session, reported to the court that Paris was exonerated. The Hartford Republican wrote that a majority of the grand jurors, nine Democrats and three Republicans, had voted against indicting him. Black residents, according to the Courier-Journal's Hartford correspondent, expressed "some dissatisfaction" with the decision, but no further trouble was expected.

The first and fullest report was an Owensboro special in the Courier-Journal of May 17, headlined "NEGROES Threaten To Make Trouble At Hartford" with the deck "RACE WAR SEEMS PROBABLE." It centered the story on an expected Black "outbreak," called Render "a desperate character," and gave the marshal's version as fact. Its opening ran the same day in the Wichita Daily Eagle under "TROUBLE EXPECTED," and a shorter wire saying fears of a "race war" had passed appeared in the Indianapolis Journal on May 18 and the Ohio Democrat on May 21.

The local Hartford Herald ran its account on May 20 under "NEGRO KILLED," called Render's companions "darkies," and said its narrative was the one Paris gave its reporter. It dismissed the city papers' accounts as the work of "some irresponsible reporter here." The grand jury's decision drew only a brief Courier-Journal item and a line in Republican court notes.
In the Black press, the Western World of Oklahoma City reprinted the opening of the Louisville dispatch, extermination threat included, in a "Kentucky News" column on May 21 without comment.

The accounts differ on whether Render was armed: the Courier-Journal said he was known to be armed and reached toward his pocket, while the Herald said no weapon was found on his body. Both rest on the officer's side, but the Herald's is local and later. They also differ on the scale of the unrest, which the Herald said "did not last long," and on the marshal's name, given as R. L. Paris, Enon Paris and R. L. Parris.

reader.title: Killing of Andrew Render
bases: Render was shot dead by Hartford's town marshal, who said he was trying to quiet a crowd and threatened arrest, and who surrendered to the sheriff (A1, A4).

The Courier-Journal's Owensboro special, the local Hartford Herald, the Courier-Journal's Hartford special and the Hartford Republican agree that Marshal Paris shot and killed Render and was not indicted (A1, A4, A7, A8), though the account of why he fired comes only from Paris's side.

accounts.label: Owensboro special (Courier-Journal)
accounts.gist: Render cursed the marshal, said no one could arrest him and reached toward his back pocket, and Paris fired; 150 armed Black men then gathered and armed whites threatened to exterminate the county's Black population.

accounts.label: Marshal Paris (via Hartford Herald)
accounts.gist: Render walked out of a noisy crowd, said Paris could not arrest him, and advanced with one hand behind him; Paris feared for his life and shot him; no weapon was found on the body.

accounts.label: Render's lodge members (as reported)
accounts.gist: Render had been 'shot down for nothing'; they said they would mob Paris before morning.

accounts.label: Grand jury
accounts.gist: A majority voted against indicting Paris, and the report to the court exonerated him.

framing.detail: Courier-Journal headlines 'NEGROES Threaten To Make Trouble At Hartford' and 'RACE WAR SEEMS PROBABLE'; calls Render 'a desperate character' and gives the marshal's account as fact.
Hartford Herald 'NEGRO KILLED. Marshal Paris Shot Andy Render While the Latter Was Advancing Upon Him'; uses 'darkies'; states the account is Paris's own and scorns the city papers' sensationalism.
Wichita Daily Eagle 'TROUBLE EXPECTED. Negro Killed by Marshal Causes Much Bad Feeling.'
Louisville wire 'No Fear of Race War' / 'Feared a Race War' casts the danger as Black residents trying 'to lynch the officer.'
Brief notices of the grand jury outcome: 'Marshal Parris Exonerated' and a line in the Hartford Republican's court notes.
Western World reprints the opening of the Louisville dispatch, including the extermination threat, in a 'Kentucky News' column without comment.
